stories.headline: Aurora City Council halts effort to reconsider data center moratorium amid Trident fight
stories.summary:
Aurora City Council shut down an effort to reconsider a data center moratorium Monday night, amid boos and cries from residents. A motion to suspend council rules failed 6-5 just before midnight. Council members Rob Andrews, Françoise Bergen, Curtis Gardner, Stephanie Hancock and Angela Lawson voted no, leaving supporters short of the seven votes needed to proceed under current rules.

The vote is the latest setback in a long fight over the proposed 900,000-square-foot Trident data center, which would sit near Aurora homes and on Denver's border. Public comment stretched into the early hours of Tuesday. Denver City Council member Stacie Gilmore, an outspoken critic of the site, told Aurora leaders that others have moratoriums because there are no laws to regulate such facilities.

Over the summer, the council rejected a six-month moratorium, with Mayor Mike Coffman casting the tie-breaking vote. Coffman now supports an indefinite moratorium, saying the Trident proposal changed his view and that current regulations are inadequate. He said he will bring the same motion back at the next regular council meeting.

stories.headline: Two college students missing after snowstorm near Buena Vista; tent found at Lake Ann
stories.summary:
Search teams from multiple counties are looking for two Colorado Mountain College students who went hiking near Buena Vista over the weekend and have not returned. Kaden Matsuda, 19, and Jackson Donlon, 20, were reported missing Monday after staff at the Leadville campus learned they had left days earlier. They had planned to hike Ice Mountain, a very technical route in northern Chaffee County.

Deputies found Matsuda's car at the Mt. Huron trailhead Monday. They believe the men arrived Friday and camped before a Saturday storm dropped about 8 inches of snow at the trailhead and 1 to 2 feet on Ice Mountain. Helicopters, drones and infrared aircraft searched Monday without finding the men or footprints.

About 50 searchers from five counties resumed Tuesday, and at noon a helicopter spotted the hikers' collapsed tent near Lake Ann, at about 12,000 feet. Sleeping bags, a stove and some clothing were inside, but the men were not. Sheriff Andy Rohrich said he remains optimistic, noting that Matsuda is studying to be a wildland firefighter and Donlon a mountain guide, but warned poor weather is expected again later this week.

stories.headline: Denver among seven finalists to host NCAA men's Final Four between 2032 and 2036
stories.summary:
The NCAA announced Tuesday that Denver is one of seven cities under consideration to host the Division I men's basketball Final Four between 2032 and 2036. The other finalists are Houston, Indianapolis, Kansas City, Las Vegas, Nashville and New Orleans.

Denver hosted the Final Four once before, in 1990, when UNLV beat Duke 103-73 at McNichols Sports Arena. The city has also hosted early-round games in several years, most recently 2023 and 2025, and regionals in 1985, 1989 and 1996. Since 1997 the NCAA has played the Final Four in football stadiums.

Denver officials tied the bid to the proposed new Broncos stadium at Burnham Yard, which the team has targeted for the 2031 NFL season. Mayor Mike Johnston said a stadium with a retractable roof and more than 50,000 seats would expand the city's eligibility for such events. Denver Sports Commission director Matthew Payne said the news shows the importance of the new stadium.

stories.headline: Denver rental assistance faces 70% funding drop in Johnston's 2027 budget
stories.summary:
Denver residents urged city leaders Monday not to cut the Temporary Rental and Utility Assistance program during a public hearing on Mayor Mike Johnston's proposed 2027 budget. The program offers up to six months of help, and the average beneficiary receives about $7,300, according to the Community Economic Defense Project, a nonprofit that administers it.

The 2026 budget set aside $15.1 million for the program, compared with $4.5 million committed for 2027, a $10.6 million or about 70% reduction. The administration says the money funds the program through June. Johnston declined the City Council's request for an additional $5.5 million, saying the city will await a Harvard University evaluation.

Johnston has proposed a $1.684 billion 2027 general operating budget, a 1.1% increase over this year. The council must adopt the budget by Nov. 9. Advocates argue evictions are a major risk factor for homelessness, the mayor's signature issue, and note that federal pandemic relief funding has dried up.

stories.headline: Toddler missing nearly a year found safe in Denver; grandfather arrested
stories.summary:
A toddler missing for nearly a year was found safe earlier this month at a home in Denver's Montbello neighborhood, and the child's grandfather was arrested on suspicion of kidnapping. The El Paso County Sheriff's Office said the child's legal guardian reported in November that the mother, 30-year-old Aleyha Murphy, had refused to comply with a court order to return the child.

Deputies made several attempts to find Murphy and the child without success. Colorado Springs police arrested Murphy in August, but the child was not with her. A search warrant for her home led investigators to the Denver address.

Aurora police and Denver Metro SWAT arrested 54-year-old David McGhee on Oct. 8. He faces charges of second-degree kidnapping, attempt to influence a public servant and harboring a minor. Murphy faces a charge of violating a court-ordered custody arrangement. The child was returned to the custodial parent.

stories.headline: Why Denver's 4% inflation may feel much higher
stories.summary:
The Denver area's annual inflation rate was 4% in September, but many residents and businesses say costs feel much higher. The consumer price index tracks a fixed basket of goods, so it may not match any one person's spending. Gas prices rose 29% over the year, household furnishings 3.6% and alcoholic beverages 5.8%, while used car prices fell 1.4%.

Since the war in Iran began Feb. 28, a gallon of unleaded gas in Colorado has risen 56% to $4.46, and diesel is up 90.3% to $6.61, according to AAA. Jim and Dave White, who run JFW Corp., a Commerce City trucking company with 110 trucks, said fuel is now 34% of costs, up from 23% last year.

Because fuel surcharges can only be reset every 30 days, the company absorbs increases in between. General manager Dave White said that has left the company $800,000 to $1 million short on cash. Consumers such as Loveland resident Robert Elliott described cutting back on entertainment and driving as prices climb.

stories.headline: Slumping Avalanche search for answers after lapses in effort
stories.summary:
The Colorado Avalanche have lost three of their last four games, and players say the problem is effort rather than results alone. Forward Parker Kelly cited work ethic, including his own, while captain Gabe Landeskog said the group has not been good enough and that the bad games have been very bad.

The issues began with poor execution in a loss to Philadelphia. Defeats to New Jersey and Nashville were more effort-based. The Devils held shot leads of 23-5 and 38-17 before a late Colorado push, and it was only the second time in 174 games the Avalanche allowed 40-plus shots. Nashville outshot Colorado 35-21 in a 6-2 win.

Coach Jared Bednar said he hopes players become more concerned and that urgency rises. Players expressed confidence they can return to the consistent effort that has marked the team in recent seasons.

stories.headline: Denver home healthcare company ends full-service emergency at-home care model, adds new executives
stories.summary:
A Denver-based company is ending its full-service model for emergency at-home care as it brings on new C-level executives, according to the Denver Business Journal. The shift includes a new CEO and a new CFO.

The report also notes layoffs tied to the restructuring. The company, DispatchHealth, is shifting its strategy as part of the pivot.

Further details on the scope of the layoffs and the new business direction were not available in the excerpt of the report.

stories.headline: Dense fog affects Denver morning commute; mild, dry weather ahead
stories.summary:
Dense fog reduced visibility across the Denver metro area and parts of the Front Range Tuesday morning, Oct. 27, prompting a fog advisory. The advisory covered the urban corridor including Fort Collins, Fort Morgan and Denver International Airport, and the National Weather Service said it could affect the morning commute.

More fog is possible overnight into Wednesday, especially in northeastern Colorado. The South Platte River Valley from Julesburg to Greeley is the biggest concern, with visibility potentially falling to a quarter-mile, and a Dense Fog Advisory may be needed along the I-76 corridor.

Once fog clears, Wednesday and Thursday look dry with Denver highs in the mid to upper 60s. Halloween evening should be mild, in the mid to upper 50s. Light mountain rain and snow are possible over the weekend, and a larger storm may approach early next week, though its track is uncertain.

stories.headline: Colorado's 'Mad Pooper' to be subject of TLC documentary
stories.summary:
TLC has released a trailer for an upcoming documentary about the 'Mad Pooper' of Colorado Springs, a runner accused of defecating in front of a family's home and other residences numerous times in 2017. The story went nationally viral at the time, and her identity was never publicly established.

The two-hour special, titled The Mad Pooper, airs on TLC on Nov. 19. It will be available on HBO Max and discovery+ the following day.

The trailer suggests the documentary may narrow the situation to a particular suspect, though no identification has been reported and it is unclear whether further investigation reached a conclusion.

topStory.headline: U.S. to Grant Visas to Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro and Family After Reports He Left Brazil Following Election Loss
topStory.summary:
A senior U.S. State Department official said on Tuesday that the Trump administration will issue visas to Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro and his family, allowing them to enter the United States. The announcement followed news reports that Bolsonaro had left Brazil after losing the country's presidential election. It came one day after Brazil's Supreme Court ordered him to surrender his passports as part of an investigation into alleged money laundering.

Bolsonaro, the son of former right-wing president Jair Bolsonaro, has denied any wrongdoing. On Monday he said he had "never thought about leaving the country" and would remain in Brazil to lead the opposition. He lost the election by more than 4.4 million votes. He initially refused to acknowledge the result and said he would seek its annulment, but his party issued a statement on Monday saying it accepted the outcome.

President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, speaking in Brasilia during celebrations of his 81st birthday, criticized the senator's departure. "A person who sneaks out of their country must have something to hide," he said, adding that leaving Brazil was "shameful" and that Bolsonaro should have stayed to prove his innocence. Lula also said Brazil is the Bolsonaro family's "second country" while the United States is their first. He has previously accused members of the family of courting U.S. interference in Brazilian affairs for political gain.

U.S. President Donald Trump responded to the election by casting doubt on the result, telling reporters it "looked like another rigged election." No evidence has emerged that the vote was marred by malfeasance. Critics pointed to a last-minute decision to extend polling hours, but Lula's victory was commanding and the extension was considered unlikely to have changed the outcome.

Democratic Representative Joaquin Castro said Trump should tell Congress whether his administration played a role in Bolsonaro's exit. "Losing an election is not grounds for asylum," Castro said, noting that Bolsonaro is under investigation for alleged corruption, money laundering and currency evasion. Bolsonaro's younger brother, Eduardo, who lives in the U.S. and was convicted in absentia in June for illegally lobbying the Trump administration, said in a podcast interview earlier this month that Flavio should leave Brazil if he lost the race. The episode is likely to add strain to relations between Washington and Brasilia, and questions remain over how Brazilian courts will respond to the senator's absence.
